newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy reform commission submerged by amendments.
newsitem.headline: Italy reform commission submerged by amendments.

text.p: The head of an Italian commission looking into much-needed constitutional reforms said on Wednesday that political parties had lodged so many amendments to key proposals that voting on them all would be impossible.

Massimo d'Alema, commission president and leader of the main Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) in the centre-left government, said parties should cut the number of amendments and proposed a delay in voting on them.
"We have before us 430 amendments on the nature of the state alone," D'Alema said.

"It will be tough to look at them one by one. But the commission must vote by June 30 and, if it does not manage to examine and vote on every amendment, I will call in the end for the basic texts to be voted on directly," he said.

He said the commission could do its work properly if the parties cut the number of amendments on the five basic texts covering the nature of the state, parliament, Europe, the form of government and the judicial system.
To that end, he proposed delaying any voting on amendments to June 17 from Wednesday.

He also suggested incorporating some key amendments in the basic texts, which were adopted last week as a preliminary recommendation for reform, and then voting on them. The commission's final vote is scheduled for June 30.
The proposals that emerge from the cross-party commission will be debated by the full parliament, along with any further amendments, and eventually put to a national referendum.
The 70-member commission was set up earlier this year to map out constitutional reform in a bid to halt the revolving-door governments which have plagued Italy since World War Two.
Modern Italian governments have lasted just 11 months on average and Italy is now on its 55th since the war.
D'Alema warned on Tuesday that the success of the reform commission was not guaranteed and said failure would be a blow for the whole country.

Italy's post-war constitution, designed to make sure no-one could ever again be as powerful as Fascist dictator Benito Mussolini, provides for a largely symbolic head of state, while the government is entirely responsible for policy initiatives.
In a key vote in the commission last week, centre-right opposition parties succeeded in getting backing for the direct election of a president, who will govern alongside a parliamentary premier.
Centre-left parties had wanted to reinforce the powers of the prime minister and leave the president with a largely symbolic role, as is now the case.
